# Feature Specification: Core Game — Syncro

**Feature Branch**: `001-core-game-spec`
**Created**: 2026-05-10
**Status**: Active
**Branch Scope**: Project skeleton — domain data structures, interfaces, and module layout
**Input**: Project bootstrap — full game vision for Syncro traffic-light optimisation game

## User Scenarios & Testing *(mandatory)*

> **Scope of this branch**: The user stories below describe the complete game vision that guides all architectural decisions. This branch (`001-core-game-spec`) delivers only the project skeleton — module layout, build configuration, sealed class hierarchies, data classes, and interface stubs — with no simulation logic, UI, or game behavior implemented. Subsequent branches will implement the stories.

### User Story 1 — Living City with Traffic Simulation (Priority: P1)

The player opens the game and sees a procedurally generated city. Roads, intersections, and
buildings fill the screen. Vehicles spawn from residential buildings each morning, navigate the
city using shortest-path routing, and return home each evening. The city feels alive: cars queue
at intersections, travel along roads, and the density visibly grows over time. The game ends when
a gridlock condition is triggered (a critical proportion of vehicles are stuck indefinitely).

**Why this priority**: Without a working simulation, no other feature is testable or meaningful.
This is the engine that every other user story sits on.

**Independent Test**: Launch the game and observe 5 in-game minutes without interacting. Verify
that vehicles spawn, move, queue, re-route, and that gridlock eventually occurs if left
unattended.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** a fresh game start, **When** the morning rush hour begins (07:00), **Then** vehicles
   spawn from residential buildings and navigate towards destination buildings using A* routing.
2. **Given** vehicles travelling the road network, **When** an intersection has no traffic
   light, **Then** vehicles must resolve conflicts manually (right-of-way yields), causing visible
   queuing and delay.
3. **Given** all vehicles are immovable (complete gridlock), **When** the gridlock threshold is
   sustained for 10 consecutive in-game seconds, **Then** the game-over screen is shown.
4. **Given** a road lane with all cells occupied, **When** an additional vehicle attempts to
   enter the last cell, **Then** the vehicle remains in its current cell (Nagel–Schreckenberg
   blocking rule) and the cell occupancy ratio for that edge reaches 1.0.

---

### User Story 2 — Traffic Light Management (Priority: P2)

The player taps or clicks on any intersection to open its upgrade panel. They can install a
traffic light system (fixed-time signals) and manually adjust the phase timing and green/red
durations for each signal phase. They can observe the queue at that intersection shrink or grow
depending on their settings. More advanced sensor tiers (inductive loop detector, traffic
camera) unlock automated phase adjustments.

**Why this priority**: This is the central mechanic of the game — everything else is built around
it. Without the ability to control intersections, there is no player agency.

**Independent Test**: Open an intersection panel, install a fixed-time signal, change the phase
timing, and verify the queue length at that intersection visibly changes compared to an
unmodified intersection nearby.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** an intersection in manual-control mode, **When** the player upgrades it to fixed-time signals,
   **Then** the intersection cycles through its phases at the configured timing and vehicles
   receive right-of-way in turns.
2. **Given** a manual-control intersection, **When** the player upgrades to an inductive loop
   detector, **Then** phases with no waiting vehicles are skipped automatically.
3. **Given** a camera-equipped intersection, **When** queue lengths differ between approaches,
   **Then** the system extends green time proportionally to the longest queue without player
   input.
4. **Given** an intersection with Phase Skip automation, **When** a signal phase has zero
   queued vehicles, **Then** that phase is automatically skipped and the cycle advances.

---

### User Story 3 — Real-Time Performance Metrics HUD (Priority: P3)

A graph in the top corner of the screen continuously plots four traffic performance metrics:
control delay, queue length, throughput, and volume-to-capacity ratio. The graph updates in
real time. The player can observe the metrics worsen during rush hours and improve immediately
after they make a beneficial traffic light adjustment.

**Why this priority**: Metrics provide the feedback loop that teaches the player whether their
actions are helping. Without this, the optimisation aspect is opaque.

**Independent Test**: Apply a traffic light upgrade to a bottleneck intersection and verify that
at least one metric visibly improves on the graph within the next 60 in-game seconds compared to
the pre-upgrade trend.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** the HUD is visible, **When** a rush hour window starts, **Then** all four metrics
   trend upward on the graph within 30 in-game seconds.
2. **Given** a player optimises a congested intersection, **When** the improvement takes effect,
   **Then** control delay and queue length trend downward on the graph within 60 in-game seconds.
3. **Given** the player applies a greenway across a corridor, **When** vehicles start using it,
   **Then** throughput on that corridor increases and is reflected in the global throughput metric.

---

### User Story 4 — Day/Night Cycle and City Growth (Priority: P4)

The game simulates a full 24-hour day cycle. During the day, rush hours increase vehicle density
and challenge. At night, vehicle density drops to near zero and the player can freely adjust
infrastructure without the pressure of live traffic. Each morning, a "car dealership" animation
plays showing new vehicles being added to new homes, and the city map visibly expands with new
roads, intersections, and buildings added to its edges.

**Why this priority**: The day/night rhythm creates pacing, gives the player breathing room for
planning, and makes city growth feel rewarding rather than punishing.

**Independent Test**: Survive two full in-game days. Verify that: (a) rush hours produce
noticeably higher congestion, (b) the night phase is calm enough to adjust signals without
pressure, and (c) the city map is larger and contains more vehicles on day 2 than day 1.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** in-game time reaching 07:00, **When** the morning rush hour begins, **Then** vehicle
   spawn rate increases at least 3× compared to the off-peak rate.
2. **Given** the in-game clock passing 22:00, **When** night phase begins, **Then** all active
   vehicles complete their journeys and no new vehicles spawn until 07:00.
3. **Given** the end of a day, **When** the night transition plays, **Then** a dealership
   animation spawns new vehicles at dealership buildings and those vehicles register to new
   residential homes.
4. **Given** a new morning starting, **When** the player reviews the city map, **Then** at least
   one new road segment, intersection, and building have been added to the city edge compared to
   the prior day.
5. **Given** a city running for 5+ days, **When** a redevelopment event triggers, **Then** a
   district closes visually (construction overlay), remains unavailable for 1–2 days, and
   reopens with a different building type (e.g., residential → commercial).

---

### User Story 5 — Greenways (Priority: P5)

The player can draw a greenway path by swiping/dragging across connected road segments. The
intersections along the path synchronize their signal phases so that a platoon of vehicles
entering the greenway at a green light continues through every subsequent intersection without
stopping. The player can visually see vehicles travelling the greenway corridor without stopping,
and can delete or redraw greenways at any time — day or night.

**Why this priority**: Greenways are the highest-complexity player tool and the primary
differentiator from simple traffic-light games. They require active spatial thinking and deliver
a satisfying visual result.

**Independent Test**: Draw a greenway across 3 consecutive intersections on a busy corridor.
Observe that vehicles entering on green pass all three intersections without stopping, and
throughput on that corridor increases by a measurable amount.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** the player draws a greenway path across 3+ connected intersections, **When** the
   gesture is confirmed, **Then** the affected intersections coordinate their phase offsets to
   create a continuous green window for vehicles travelling the greenway direction.
2. **Given** a greenway is active, **When** a vehicle platoon enters the corridor on a green
   phase, **Then** each subsequent intersection on the greenway is green when that platoon
   arrives.
3. **Given** an active greenway, **When** the player deletes it, **Then** the intersections
   revert to their independent timing immediately.
4. **Given** two conflicting greenways share an intersection, **When** both are active,
   **Then** the game notifies the player of the conflict and does not apply both simultaneously.

---

### User Story 6 — Events System (Priority: P6)

Random events occur during the day. An emergency vehicle appears at a map edge and must reach
a destination across the city; every second it spends waiting at a red light incurs a score
penalty. Road accidents temporarily block one road segment. Players with Priority Mode installed
at an intersection can instantly green-light the emergency vehicle. Players who purchased the
Accident Cleaning upgrade can resolve accidents faster.

**Why this priority**: Events add unpredictability and reward players who have invested in the
right upgrades, reinforcing the upgrade system's value.

**Independent Test**: Trigger an emergency vehicle event manually in debug mode. Verify that
(a) without Priority Mode the vehicle waits in normal queue order and a penalty counter
increments, and (b) with Priority Mode the vehicle receives instant green and the penalty
counter stays at zero.

**Acceptance Scenarios**:

1. **Given** an emergency vehicle event starts, **When** the vehicle reaches an intersection
   without Priority Mode, **Then** it waits in the normal queue and a penalty score accumulates
   per second of waiting.
2. **Given** an intersection has Priority Mode installed, **When** an emergency vehicle
   approaches, **Then** all conflicting phases are immediately halted and the emergency vehicle
   receives a green light.
3. **Given** an accident event on a road segment, **When** it triggers, **Then** that segment
   is visually marked as blocked and vehicles reroute around it.
4. **Given** the player has Accident Cleaning upgrade, **When** an accident occurs, **Then**
   a prompt allows the player to pay the per-use cost and clear the accident in half the normal
   duration.

---

### Edge Cases

- What happens when a greenway path passes through an intersection in manual-control mode?
  (The greenway cannot be applied; the player is notified that the intersection must first be
  upgraded to at least fixed-time automation before a greenway phase offset can be set.)
- What happens when a vehicle's A* route is blocked by an accident and no alternative route
  exists? (The vehicle waits in place; this contributes to gridlock build-up.)
- What happens when a city expansion adds a road segment that bisects an existing greenway?
  (The greenway is invalidated and the player is notified to redraw it.)
- What happens during an emergency event if Priority Mode is installed but the intersection's
  current phase cannot be interrupted (e.g., during a phase transition)? (The emergency vehicle
  receives priority at the start of the next half-cycle, ensuring maximum 5-second delay.)
- What happens if two emergency vehicles are active simultaneously?
  (Each is tracked independently; penalties accumulate for each vehicle separately.)
- What happens to upgrades when a district enters redevelopment?
  (All upgrade costs are refunded to the player's currency balance; greenways crossing the
  district are invalidated with a player notification.)

## Requirements *(mandatory)*

### Functional Requirements

**City & Roads**

- **FR-001**: The game MUST procedurally generate a tile-based city grid containing road
  tiles, intersection tiles, building tiles, and empty tiles each new session.
- **FR-003**: Each pair of adjacent intersection tiles connected by road tiles MUST be
  represented as two directed topology edges (one per direction). Each edge is a sequence
  of Nagel–Schreckenberg cells; cell count is hard-coded per tile type and direction
  (e.g., a turn tile has fewer cells on the inner lane than the outer lane).
- **FR-003a**: The NS model physics parameters — maximum vehicle speed (`vMax`, in cells
  per tick) and spontaneous deceleration probability (`dawdlingProbability`) — MUST be
  global constants stored in `BalanceConfig`. All edges share these defaults in the initial
  implementation; per-edge overrides are out of scope for the skeleton branch.
- **FR-004**: The game MUST support exactly three intersection tile types: 4-way (X),
  3-way (T, four rotations), and roundabout. Each type exposes typed input/output ports,
  hard-coded internal paths, and a hard-coded set of signal phases determined by the tile
  type. Non-roundabout intersections have a conflict matrix encoding which internal paths
  cannot be simultaneously active; roundabouts have no conflict matrix.
- **FR-005**: Roundabouts MUST be modelled as an intersection with exactly one signal phase
  in which all internal paths are simultaneously green-lit. Vehicle conflict at roundabout
  entry MUST be resolved by Nagel–Schreckenberg cell-occupancy blocking (a vehicle cannot
  enter an already-occupied cell); no explicit conflict matrix or yield rule is required.

**Vehicle Simulation**

- **FR-006**: Each vehicle MUST have a persistent home building; it leaves home each morning
  and returns to a destination building during the day. In the evening, vehicles MUST return
  to a building: home is strongly preferred, but public multi-level garages are a valid
  alternative return destination. Return destination MUST be selected by a probability map
  that makes home significantly more likely than any public garage.
- **FR-007**: Destination assignment MUST be probabilistic. The final probability for any
  candidate building MUST be the product of two independent factors:
  1. **Type weight** — a per-building-type multiplier that varies by time-of-day (e.g.,
     office buildings weighted highest during morning rush, residential highest in the evening,
     multi-level garages as a low-weight alternative return destination).
  2. **Spatial weight** — a 2D Gaussian probability map centered on the city center; buildings
     closer to the center have higher spatial weight, making central offices and amenities
     significantly more attractive destinations than equivalent buildings at the city edge.
- **FR-052**: The Gaussian spatial map's sigma MUST scale proportionally with the current city
  radius so that edge buildings remain reachable as the city expands; a fixed sigma would
  make peripheral buildings unreachable in large cities.
- **FR-053**: The Gaussian center coordinates, base sigma, sigma-to-radius scaling factor, and
  all per-building-type time-of-day weights MUST be defined as constants in BalanceConfig to
  allow tuning without modifying simulation logic.
- **FR-049**: Vehicles MUST NOT visibly disappear in open space. The rendering layer MUST
  interpolate vehicle positions between simulation ticks to produce smooth motion, and MUST
  play an appropriate entry animation when a vehicle reaches its destination entrance cell.
- **FR-050**: Each building MUST track the count of vehicles currently parked inside it. A
  building MUST NOT release (spawn outgoing) vehicles unless its internal parked count is
  greater than zero. This conservation rule ensures no vehicle appears from a building it
  never entered.
- **FR-008**: Vehicles MUST compute routes using the A* pathfinding algorithm on the topology
  graph; edge weight is proportional to cell count. *(A* deferred: branch 003 implements
  Dijkstra as the correct heuristic-free baseline; A* with a spatial heuristic is planned for
  a future routing-optimisation branch once tile-position coordinates are exposed on topology
  nodes.)*
- **FR-009**: Vehicles MAY only enter an intersection path if that path is in the current
  phase's `greenPaths` and no conflicting path is occupied (conflict matrix rule). Vehicles
  that cannot advance remain in their current cell (Nagel–Schreckenberg blocking).
- **FR-010**: A vehicle MUST NOT enter an intersection path unless the cell chain leading
  to its exit node is clear enough to complete the traversal; this prevents junction blocking.
- **FR-011**: The game MUST detect gridlock when ≥ 60% of all active vehicles have been
  stationary for ≥ 10 consecutive in-game seconds and display the game-over screen.

**Traffic Light Management**

- **FR-012**: Every intersection MUST start the game in manual-control mode: the player
  directly selects which signal phase is active. The available phase set is hard-coded by
  tile type and never changes regardless of upgrade tier.
- **FR-013**: Players MUST be able to upgrade an intersection's signal automation in sequence:
  Manual → Fixed-time → Inductive-loop → Traffic Camera. Each tier automates phase
  selection; the available phase set is unaffected by the upgrade.
- **FR-014**: Players MUST be able to configure phase durations on any intersection operating
  in fixed-time or higher automation mode.
- **FR-015**: Inductive-loop intersections MUST automatically skip phases with no waiting
  vehicles.
- **FR-016**: Traffic-camera intersections MUST automatically extend green time proportionally
  to the measured queue length.
- **FR-017**: Players MUST be able to add Phase Skip automation to any intersection operating
  in automated mode (fixed-time or higher).
- **FR-018**: Players MUST be able to add Priority Mode automation to any intersection
  operating in automated mode (fixed-time or higher).

**Greenways**

- **FR-019**: Players MUST be able to create a greenway by drawing a continuous path over
  connected road segments via swipe/drag gesture (mouse on desktop, touch on mobile).
- **FR-020**: Intersections along a greenway MUST synchronize signal phase offsets so vehicles
  entering on green pass all downstream intersections without stopping.
- **FR-021**: Each intersection on a greenway MUST be operating in fixed-time automation or
  higher; creating a greenway over an intersection in manual-control mode MUST be blocked
  with an explanatory prompt.
- **FR-022**: Players MUST be able to delete a greenway at any time; affected intersections
  MUST revert to independent timing immediately.
- **FR-023**: Conflicting greenways sharing an intersection MUST not be simultaneously applied;
  the game MUST notify the player and allow them to choose which takes priority.

**Day/Night Cycle & City Growth**

- **FR-024**: The game MUST simulate a 24-hour cycle with three rush-hour phases:
  `MORNING_RUSH` (07:00–09:00), `MIDDAY_RUSH` (14:00–16:00), and `EVENING_RUSH` (17:00–20:00).
  Off-peak day time (`MIDDAY`, covering 09:00–14:00 and 16:00–17:00) and `NIGHT` (20:00–07:00)
  are the remaining phases.
- **FR-025**: Vehicle spawn rate MUST be at least 3× higher during all three rush-hour phases
  (`MORNING_RUSH`, `MIDDAY_RUSH`, `EVENING_RUSH`) than during off-peak phases.
- **FR-026**: The night phase (22:00–06:00) MUST have near-zero vehicle spawns, giving the
  player uninterrupted infrastructure management time.
- **FR-027**: At the end of each day, the game MUST introduce new vehicles via a dealership
  animation; new vehicles MUST be assigned to new residential homes.
- **FR-028**: After each day, the procedural generator MUST append new roads, intersections,
  and buildings to the city boundary. There is no hard cap on city size.
- **FR-028a**: Vehicle count MUST grow according to a polynomial function of the current day:
  `vehicles_added = round(f(day) × rng)` where `f(day) = vehicleCountBase + vehicleCountGrowthPerDay × day`
  and `rng` is a random factor within `±vehicleCountRngVariance` of 1.0. The initial vehicle
  count at Day 0 is `vehicleCountBase`. All three coefficients MUST be stored in `BalanceConfig`.
  Vehicle growth rate MUST outpace city tile growth so vehicle density increases over time.
- **FR-029**: City redevelopment events MUST occasionally transform a district (1–2 days of
  construction closure) into a different building type.
- **FR-048**: When a redevelopment event begins, the game MUST automatically refund the full
  currency cost of all upgrades installed on intersections within the affected district;
  any greenways passing through that district MUST be invalidated and the player notified.
- **FR-045**: The player MUST be able to pause the game at any time; while paused, the
  simulation freezes completely and the player retains full access to the infrastructure
  management UI. Pause is implemented by stopping the game loop from firing ticks; no
  domain entity carries a paused flag.
- **FR-046**: The day phase MUST NOT offer any fast-forward or time-skip control; day pacing
  MUST be tuned (via BalanceConfig) such that the player always has meaningful decisions to
  make.
- **FR-047**: The night phase MUST offer a single "Skip to Morning" control; activating it
  advances in-game time to 07:00 by increasing the game-loop tick rate to 4× normal,
  accompanied by a visible time-lapse animation. The simulation engine is invoked exactly as
  usual — only the loop cadence changes.
- **FR-054**: The simulation engine MUST be speed-agnostic: one engine tick equals exactly
  one NS model progression; the engine MUST NOT reference or store any real-world elapsed
  time, wall-clock rate, or speed multiplier.
- **FR-055**: Simulation tick rate and speed multiplier MUST be controlled exclusively by
  the game loop (app layer). At normal play speed the loop MUST fire 6–8 simulation ticks
  per real-world second. Speed-up modes MUST increase ticks per second at the loop level
  without modifying any domain entity or `BalanceConfig` value.
- **FR-056**: One full in-game 24-hour day MUST complete in ≤ 3 real-world minutes at
  normal simulation speed. The total tick count for one in-game day (`BalanceConfig.
  ticksPerInGameDay`) MUST be calibrated to satisfy this constraint at the configured
  normal tick rate.
- **FR-057**: NS cell counts MUST be derived from `TileType` and path direction at
  topology-graph derivation time. Road-lane edges: straight tile = 3 cells per lane; turn tile
  outer arc = 4 cells; turn tile inner arc = 3 cells. Internal intersection path edges:
  straight-through = 3 cells; right-turn = 3 cells (inner arc equivalent); left-turn = 4 cells
  (outer arc equivalent). All six constants MUST be stored in `BalanceConfig` so they can be
  tuned without modifying construction logic.
- **FR-058**: The rendering layer MUST produce smooth vehicle animation at ≥ 60 frames per
  second by interpolating between consecutive simulation state snapshots. The architecture
  MUST support display refresh rates above 60 Hz without changes to the simulation or
  game-loop layers.

**Performance Metrics HUD**

- **FR-030**: The game MUST display a live time-series graph showing all four metrics:
  Control Delay, Queue Length, Throughput, and Volume/Capacity Ratio.
- **FR-031**: The graph MUST update in real time, reflecting the current simulation state
  within 1 in-game second of any change.
- **FR-032**: The graph MUST be visible in the corner of the screen without obscuring the
  city; it MUST be dismissible/minimisable.

**Events**

- **FR-033**: Emergency vehicle events MUST spawn a priority vehicle that accumulates a score
  penalty for each in-game second it waits at a red light.
- **FR-034**: Accident events MUST temporarily block the affected road segment and force
  vehicles to reroute.
- **FR-035**: The Accident Cleaning upgrade MUST be available for purchase; when owned, the
  player can pay a per-use cost to halve the accident duration.

**Upgrades & Economy**

- **FR-036**: Players MUST be able to purchase the Patient Drivers global upgrade; with it
  active, vehicles avoid blocking intersections and reroute rather than gridlock.
- **FR-037**: Players MUST be able to purchase speed-limit upgrades on individual road
  segments.
- **FR-038**: Players MUST earn upgrade currency through vehicle trip completions. Each
  completed trip earns a base amount; the per-trip value MUST be multiplied by a metric
  efficiency factor derived from the current four performance metrics at the moment of
  completion (e.g., higher throughput and lower control delay increase the factor). A daily
  income cap MUST prevent exponential wealth accumulation as the city and vehicle count scale
  up. All numerical economy constants — base trip value, metric weight coefficients, daily
  income cap, and escalation-dampening factor — MUST be centralised in a `BalanceConfig`
  component so that balance experimentation requires no changes to simulation logic.
- **FR-039**: Upgrade purchases MUST be blocked when the player's upgrade currency balance is
  insufficient; the UI MUST display the current balance and the cost of each upgrade at all
  times.
- **FR-051**: All intersection upgrades (sensor tiers, automation modules) MUST apply to one
  specific intersection per purchase; there are no city-wide intersection upgrades. Each
  upgrade type MUST have a fixed currency cost defined in BalanceConfig that does not change
  with city size or purchase history. City growth creates natural spending pressure by
  increasing the number of intersections requiring individual investment.

**Scoring**

- **FR-040**: The game MUST track and display a final score on the game-over screen. The
  primary score MUST be total in-game time survived, expressed in hours and minutes (not only
  days), to provide sufficient granularity across short and long sessions.
- **FR-041**: The game-over screen MUST also display each of the four traffic performance
  metrics as a separate summary grade (e.g., a curve trend or letter grade), giving the player
  qualitative feedback beyond session length.
- **FR-042**: The scoring contract MUST be designed as an extensible interface so that future
  gamemodes (e.g., throughput-optimisation mode, eco/fuel-efficiency mode) can substitute a
  different scoring function without modifying core simulation code.

**Session Persistence**

- **FR-043**: The game MUST automatically save complete session state to local persistent
  storage whenever the player pauses the game or the application is closed or backgrounded.
- **FR-044**: On launch, if a saved session exists, the game MUST offer the player the option
  to resume it from the exact point where they left off. If the save file is incompatible
  with the current build (e.g., schema changed after an update), the game MUST discard it
  with a clear notification and offer to start a new session. No migration of old saves is
  in scope for v1.

### Key Entities

- **City**: The game world; a rectangular tile grid plus the derived topology graph and
  building registry. The tile grid grows each night.
- **TileType**: The type of a single grid tile — straight road, turn, X/T intersection,
  roundabout, building part, or empty. The topology graph is derived from tile types.
- **TopologyGraph**: The directed graph used for routing and simulation. Nodes are
  intersection input/output ports. Edges are either road lanes (spanning road tiles between
  two intersections) or internal intersection paths — all represented uniformly as sequences
  of Nagel–Schreckenberg cells.
- **TopologyIntersection**: An intersection tile in the topology layer. Owns its hard-coded
  phase set (derived from tile type), conflict matrix (empty for roundabouts), current signal
  automation tier, and optional automation modifiers.
- **SignalPhase**: One state in an intersection's hard-coded phase set. Grants right-of-way
  to a subset of internal paths (`greenPaths: Set<EdgeId>`). Roundabouts have exactly one
  phase with all internal paths in `greenPaths`.
- **SignalAutomationTier**: How the active phase is selected. Manual = player-controlled;
  FixedTime = timed cycling; InductiveLoop = timed with empty-phase skip; TrafficCamera =
  adaptive queue-proportional timing. The phase set is identical at every tier.
- **IntersectionAutomation**: Optional modifiers layered on top of any automated tier:
  PhaseSkip, PriorityMode, GreenwayNode.
- **Vehicle**: A moving agent with a home building, a current destination (`CellPos`), and
  a state (Parked / Moving / Gridlocked). Position is always a `CellPos` — a specific cell
  on a topology edge. A vehicle never exists in open space without a destination.
- **CellPos**: `(edgeId: EdgeId, cell: Int)` — the uniform vehicle position type for both
  road lanes and intersection paths.
- **Greenway**: A set of `GreenwayImplication`s: "if path X of intersection A gets green,
  then path Y of intersection B gets green `tickOffset` ticks later." Forms a DAG over
  a road corridor.
- **GameClock**: Tracks in-game time (24 h cycle), current day number, and rush-hour state.
- **TrafficEvent**: A time-limited game event; subtypes are EmergencyVehicle (with penalty
  accumulator in ticks) and Accident (with blocked topology edge).
- **PerformanceSnapshot**: A time-stamped record of four metrics at a given simulation tick;
  feeds the HUD graph.
- **UpgradeInventory**: The player's owned upgrades and current upgrade-currency balance.
  Intersection upgrades are keyed by `TilePos`.
- **Building**: Occupies `BuildingPart` tiles on the grid. Carries
  a list of entrance tiles and entrance cells (two distinct concepts):
  - **Entrance tile** (`TilePos`) — a neighbouring road tile where vehicles arrive or depart;
    produced by `CityGenerator` and stored directly in `Building.entrances`.
  - **Entrance cell** (`CellPos`) — the topology-layer cell on the road edge that overlaps
    that tile; derived from the entrance tile via `TopologyGraph` after city construction,
    and used as `Vehicle.currentDestination` by the simulation.
  Subtypes: Residential, Office, ShoppingMall, MultiLevelGarage, CarDealership.
- **BalanceConfig**: Centralised constants for economy, simulation timing (expressed in
  ticks), spatial Gaussian parameters (in tile units), upgrade costs, NS model physics
  (`vMax`, `dawdlingProbability`), and vehicle growth polynomial (`vehicleCountBase`,
  `vehicleCountGrowthPerDay`, `vehicleCountRngVariance`). All edges share the same global
  NS defaults in the skeleton; per-edge overrides are deferred to a future branch.

## Success Criteria *(mandatory)*

### Measurable Outcomes

- **SC-001**: A new player with no tutorial can understand the core traffic light adjustment
  mechanic and apply their first upgrade within 2 minutes of game start.
- **SC-002**: The game renders at ≥ 60 FPS on the reference desktop machine at early-game
  scale (≈ 200 active vehicles) via interpolation between simulation snapshots. The
  simulation itself runs at 6–8 NS ticks per real-world second — these are separate,
  independently tunable concerns. Higher display refresh rates (120, 144 Hz) MUST be
  visually smooth without additional engineering. There is no hard cap on vehicle count;
  performance at late-game scale is a future optimization target.
- **SC-003**: Applying a correctly configured greenway to a corridor of ≥ 3 intersections
  reduces the average stop time for vehicles on that corridor by ≥ 30% compared to no greenway.
- **SC-004**: Traffic performance metrics (any of the four) visibly and measurably improve on
  the HUD graph within 60 in-game seconds of the player making a beneficial intersection upgrade.
- **SC-005**: The procedural city generator produces tile-based road networks that are
  visually distinct across different playthroughs.
- **SC-006**: The day/night rhythm is balanced such that a median playtest session lasts at
  least 5 in-game days before gridlock.
- **SC-007**: ≥ 80% of playtesters can identify the gridlock game-over condition as the cause
  of session end without a prompt.
- **SC-008**: An emergency vehicle event with Priority Mode installed at the relevant
  intersection incurs zero penalty score compared to the same event at an unupgraded
  intersection.

## Clarifications

### Session 2026-05-24

- Architecture decision: `Building.entrances` is `List<TilePos>` (not `List<CellPos>`). `CityGenerator` produces entrance tiles as `TilePos` because it runs before the `TopologyGraph` exists. The corresponding `CellPos` entrance cells are derived from those `TilePos` values after `TopologyGraph` construction and used by the simulation as `Vehicle.currentDestination`. These are two canonical terms: **entrance tile** (TilePos, CityGenerator domain) and **entrance cell** (CellPos, simulation domain).
- Q: Should the spec formally distinguish "entrance tile" (TilePos) from "entrance cell" (CellPos) in the Key Entities glossary? → A: Yes. The Building entry in Key Entities now defines both terms explicitly, and `Vehicle.currentDestination` carries a comment referencing the derivation.
- Q: Should FR-049's "destination entrance cell" wording be expanded inline to reference the TilePos derivation? → A: No. "Entrance cell" is now a canonical term defined in the glossary; no inline expansion is needed in FR-049.

### Session 2026-05-23

- Decision: Branch scope narrowed to project skeleton only — module layout, build scripts,
  sealed class hierarchies, data classes, and interface stubs. No simulation logic, routing,
  city generation, or UI is implemented in this branch; those follow in subsequent branches.
- Decision: City generation is tile-based. The city world is a rectangular grid of
  `TilePos → TileType` pairs; each tile has exactly one type (straight road, turn,
  intersection variant, building part, or empty).
- Architecture decision: Each intersection tile exposes directional input and output ports
  (one per connected cardinal side). These ports are the nodes of the topology graph.
  Directed edges connect nodes in two forms: **road lane edges** span a series of road tiles
  between two intersection ports, and **internal intersection path edges** are confined to a
  single intersection tile. An X-shaped intersection has 4 input nodes, 4 output nodes, and
  12 internal path edges; a T-intersection has 3 inputs, 3 outputs, and 6 internal paths.
  The result is a weighted directed graph derived from the tile grid, rebuilt whenever the
  city changes.
- Architecture decision: Each topology edge is a fixed-length ordered list of
  Nagel–Schreckenberg cells. Cell count is determined by the tile types the edge spans and
  the direction of travel (e.g., an inner-lane curve has fewer cells than an outer-lane curve).
- Architecture decision: Simulation is fully discrete. One tick advances the
  Nagel–Schreckenberg model by one step across all edges simultaneously. The domain layer
  produces only discrete `CellPos` snapshots; it has no concept of smooth movement.
  The frontend (UI rendering layer) is entirely responsible for interpolating vehicle
  positions between consecutive snapshots, using the geometry implied by each edge's tile
  path to determine the visual trajectory.
- Architecture decision: Vehicle position is uniformly `CellPos(edgeId: EdgeId, cell: Int)`.
  A single type covers both road lane cells and internal intersection path cells, so A*
  routing, the NS model, conflict detection, and metrics all operate on the same address space.
- Q: How should incompatible save files be handled when the schema changes? → A: Discard the save with a clear notification; the player starts a new session. No version field or migration code is in scope for v1.
- Q: Does the city have a maximum size cap, and is the 200-vehicle figure a hard limit? → A: No hard cap on city size; the city grows each night until gridlock ends the session. No hard cap on vehicle count either — vehicles grow without a ceiling. The 200-vehicle figure is a performance baseline for early-game reference, not a ceiling. Vehicle count MUST grow faster than city area so that vehicle density per intersection increases over time, making the game progressively harder.
- Q: Where do Nagel–Schreckenberg physics parameters (v_max, dawdling probability p) live? → A: Global constants `vMax` and `dawdlingProbability` in `BalanceConfig` for the skeleton; all edges share the same defaults. Per-edge overrides (e.g., to support FR-037 speed-limit road upgrades) are deferred to a future branch.
- Architecture decision: Game-loop timing model. The simulation engine is fully speed-agnostic — one `SimulationEngine.tick()` call equals exactly one NS model progression; the engine has no concept of real-world elapsed time. Simulation tick rate (ticks per real-world second) and speed multipliers are exclusively GameLoop (app-layer) concerns. `speedMultiplier` does not exist in any domain entity.
- Architecture decision: Normal simulation tick rate is 6–8 NS ticks per real-world second. At the midpoint of 7 ticks/second for 180 real-world seconds (3 minutes per in-game day), one in-game day = 1260 NS ticks. This value is stored in `BalanceConfig.ticksPerInGameDay` so all domain timing constants remain tick-based without needing to know the real-world speed.
- Architecture decision: In-game day/night cycle MUST complete in ≤ 3 real-world minutes at normal simulation speed. "Skip to Morning" (night phase only) speeds up the cycle by increasing the GameLoop tick rate to 4× normal; no domain entity changes during skip.
- Architecture decision: NS cell calibration per tile type — straight road tile: 3 cells per lane; turn tile: 4 cells on the outer lane, 3 cells on the inner lane. These counts are hard-coded at graph derivation time from `TileType` and drive the visual scale of movement.
- Architecture decision: Frontend rendering targets ≥ 60 FPS via interpolation between consecutive simulation snapshots. Because rendering performs no simulation logic, the design MUST support display refresh rates above 60 Hz without architectural changes; higher-rate displays interpolate at a finer time resolution between the same pair of snapshots.
- Q: Should a `MIDDAY_RUSH` phase (14:00–16:00) be added to `DayPhase` to match FR-024's three rush windows? → A: Yes. `MIDDAY_RUSH` (14:00–16:00) is added to the enum. `MIDDAY` remains the off-peak daytime phase covering 09:00–14:00 and 16:00–17:00. The 3× spawn multiplier from FR-025 applies to all three rush phases: `MORNING_RUSH`, `MIDDAY_RUSH`, and `EVENING_RUSH`.
- Q: Can T-intersections be reconfigured between 3-state and 4-state by the player? → A: No. T-intersections are always 3-state (one phase per connected arm). The phase set is hard-coded by tile type and is never player-configurable; the contradictory "optional 4-state" assumption has been removed.
- Q: How many vehicles start on Day 1, and how does the nightly vehicle addition grow over time? → A: Vehicle count follows a polynomial: `f(day) = vehicleCountBase + vehicleCountGrowthPerDay × day`. Initial count = `f(0) = vehicleCountBase`. Each night, `round(f(day) × rng(1 ± vehicleCountRngVariance))` vehicles are added. All three coefficients live in `BalanceConfig` (defaults: base=20, growthPerDay=5, rngVariance=0.15). `newVehiclesPerNight` is removed.
- Q: How are roundabouts represented in the topology graph, and does SignalTier.Uncontrolled exist? → A: SignalTier.Uncontrolled does not exist. Every intersection tile type has a hard-coded, fixed set of signal phases; phases are intrinsic to the tile type, not configurable by the player. The starting control mode for all intersections is manual — the player directly selects which phase is active. Purchasing automation (fixed-time, inductive-loop, or camera) delegates phase selection to the simulation. A roundabout is modelled as an intersection with exactly one signal phase in which all internal paths are simultaneously green-lit; vehicle conflicts at roundabout entries are resolved entirely by Nagel–Schreckenberg cell-occupancy blocking (a vehicle cannot enter an occupied cell), so no explicit conflict matrix is needed for roundabouts.

### Session 2026-05-11

- Q: Can the player control simulation speed (pause, fast-forward)? → A: Pause available at
  all times. No free fast-forward during day — pacing is designed so the player always has
  something to do. Night phase has a single "Skip to Morning" button that plays a 4× animated
  transition forward to 07:00.
- Q: Can greenways be created/modified/deleted during the day, or only at night? → A: Greenways
  are editable (create, modify, delete) at any time — day or night.
- Q: What happens to player-purchased upgrades on intersections inside a redeveloping district?
  → A: All upgrades are refunded to the player's currency balance when demolition begins.
- Q: What does a vehicle do when it reaches its destination — despawn, park visibly, or occupy
  a named slot? → A: Vehicles visually enter their destination building (garage door for homes,
  building entrance for offices/malls/garages) and are tracked as parked inside. A building
  can only release vehicles it has previously received — no car may leave a building that has
  never had one enter. Vehicles return home each evening; public multi-level garages are a
  valid alternative return destination, governed by probability maps that heavily favour home.
- Q: Are upgrade costs fixed or do they scale with city size or purchase count? → A: Each
  upgrade type has a fixed cost. Upgrades such as sensor tiers and automations apply per
  intersection individually, so city growth naturally increases total upgrade expenditure
  without requiring price scaling.
- Design decision: Destination selection uses a 2D spatial Gaussian probability map centered
  on the city center, combined with per-building-type weights. The Gaussian sigma scales
  proportionally with the current city radius so edge buildings remain reachable as the city
  grows. All Gaussian parameters are stored in BalanceConfig.

## Assumptions

- The game is fully offline; no multiplayer, online leaderboard, or cloud sync is in scope for
  the initial version.
- Sound design and background music are out of scope for the bootstrap sprint; placeholder
  silence is acceptable.
- The initial playable target is desktop JVM; Android/mobile deployment is the next milestone
  but does not constrain initial architecture decisions beyond using Compose Multiplatform.
- There is no hard cap on vehicle count or city size; both grow indefinitely until gridlock
  ends the session. The ≈ 200-vehicle figure is used only as an early-game performance
  baseline; late-game performance is a future optimization concern.
- City maps are always procedurally generated; there is no hand-crafted map or map editor in
  scope.
- Game state MUST be persisted to local device storage on pause and on application close;
  the player can resume a suspended session at any time from the point they left off.
  Management of multiple named save slots is out of scope for v1.
- Roundabouts have exactly one signal phase (all internal paths green simultaneously); vehicle
  conflicts at entry are resolved by NS cell-occupancy blocking. They are not eligible for
  signal automation upgrades or greenways.
- The greenway draw gesture uses mouse drag on desktop and touch swipe on mobile; both MUST
  be supported through the same input abstraction.
- T-intersections are always modelled as 3-state signals (one phase per connected arm). The
  phase set is hard-coded by tile type and is never player-configurable; there is no 4-state
  T-intersection variant.
- A "district redevelopment" event affects at most one district at a time per city; concurrent
  redevelopments are not in scope for v1.
